newsitem.title: UK: SMALL BABIES AT HIGHER RISK OF DIABETES - STUDY.
newsitem.headline: SMALL BABIES AT HIGHER RISK OF DIABETES - STUDY.

text.p: French researchers said on Friday they had found more evidence that unusually small babies are at risk of diabetes.
A study of more than 230 young adults showed those who were born small tended to grow up small, and that they also tended to have higher levels of blood sugar -- a first sign of diabetes.
This could be due to the effects of retarded growth in the womb, Juliane Leger and colleagues at France's national research organisation INSERM wrote in a report in the British Medical Journal.
They were investigating initial findings that indicate small babies are at risk of diabetes.
"Affected babies are known to be at a higher than average risk of illness and death from several neonatal disorders," they wrote.

Research indicates that when babies get poor nutrition in the womb, their bodies compensate to allow them to make best use of the nutrition they do receive. One possible outcome is an increased sensitivity to glucose.
Recent studies have shown that people who received poor nutrition as foetuses and babies tend to develop diabetes when they get access to a richer diet high in sugars and fats.

Leger's group studied people born in the French city of Haguenau. "After sex and target height were adjusted for, subjects who had been born small for gestational age were significantly shorter at age 20 than those with a normal birth weight," they wrote.
They also had much more trouble processing glucose -- indicating their bodies were resistant to the effects of insulin -- an early sign of diabetes.
People born small might have to take more care than usual to avoid developing diabetes, they said, "for example by preventing obesity".
